citations.narrative:
The facility continues to exceed the maximum number of animals allowed under their license. The facility is approved for
up to 100 animals, but 136 animals were documented during the inspection. The USDA license authorizes a specific
number of animals to ensure that the facility and personnel possess adequate facilities, employees and education to
provide sufficient husbandry to the regulated animals. A licensee must obtain a new license before any change resulting
in more than the authorized number of animals on hand at any single point in time during the period of licensure. The
licensee must reapply for a license that properly reflects the number of regulated animals under the license or reduce the
number of regulated animals to a number which is under the maximum threshold authorized under the current license.

citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility failed to notify the attending veterinarian about multiple animal health conditions reported by employees and
observed by APHIS inspectors. A male Toco toucan is limping due to a mass growing on its right foot. A Nanday parakeet
was observed squinting his right eye. A Variegated squirrel has hair loss along the center of its tail. Employees have
reported these conditions to the facility manager previously. The APHIS inspector also observed an Eclectus parrot with
feather loss on its chest and a male Red kangaroo to be underweight and has missing patches of hair on his chest and
along his tail.
Effective and timely communication between licensees, their employees, and the attending veterinarian is essential to
safeguarding the health and welfare of all animals. Prompt updates and collaboration can prevent problems from
escalating—many illnesses can be addressed quickly and effectively with immediate notification to the veterinarian.
Each dealer or exhibitor shall establish and maintain programs of adequate veterinary care that include the use of
appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries, and the availability of emergency,
weekend, and holiday care. To be corrected this day, July 7, 2026, forward.

The record of animals on hand (inventory) was not current. The following animals were missing from the inventory: two
Green Cheeked conures, one Umbrella cockatoo, numerous chickens, and a Zebu calf born on the premises. There was
no record of deposition for a Cape Barren goose, Ring-tailed lemur, two cows, multiple goats and the date of death for an
Indian Ringneck parrot, Black lorikeet, Rainbow lorikeet, Budgie parakeet, and Muntjac deer.
Complete and accurate records are necessary to facilitate the tracking of animals and maintain compliance with other
aspects of the AWA.
The licensee shall make, keep, and maintain records or forms which fully disclose the information concerning animals,
purchased or otherwise acquired, owned, held, leased, or otherwise in his or her possession or under his or her control, or
which is transported, sold, euthanized, or otherwise disposed of by that dealer or exhibitor. This record must be kept
current and maintained to accurately reflect all the animals.

The facility failed to maintain the flooring in a rabbit enclosure. The wire flooring in a white rabbits enclosure was exposed
and has sharp points that could potentially injure the rabbit.
Sharp, exposed wire can inflict physical harm, cause pain, infection, and behavioral distress.
All primary enclosures for rabbits shall conform to the following requirements: The floors of the primary enclosures shall
be constructed so as to protect the rabbits feet and legs from injury. Litter shall be provided in all primary enclosures
having solid floors. To be corrected this day, July 7, 2026, forward.

The facility, which houses primates in outdoor enclosures, continues to lack an adequate perimeter fence. The perimeter
fence continues to be less than 6 feet tall.
An inadequate perimeter fence leaves the facility vulnerable, creating opportunities for intruders or wild animals to enter
and potentially compromises the safety and well-being of the animals.
An outdoor housing facility must be enclosed by a fence that is of sufficient height to keep unwanted species out. The
fence must be constructed so that it protects nonhuman primates by restricting unauthorized humans, and animals the
size of dogs, skunks, and raccoons from going through it or under it and having contact with the nonhuman primates. It
must be of sufficient distance (at least 3 feet) from the outside wall or fence of the primary enclosure to prevent physical
contact between animals inside the enclosure and outside the perimeter fence.

The facility, which houses a sloth, genets, kangaroos, wallabies, kinkajous and porcupines in outdoor enclosures,
continues to lack an adequate perimeter fence. Most of the premises continue to be surrounded by a perimeter fence that
is less than 6 feet tall and has significant gaps through or underneath the fencing.
An inadequate perimeter fence leaves the facility vulnerable, creating opportunities for intruders or wild animals to enter
and potentially compromises the safety and well-being of the animals. A perimeter fence protects animals from contact
with unauthorized people and animals. A perimeter fence also acts as a secondary containment system if an animal
escapes from its primary enclosure.
All outdoor housing facilities (i.e., facilities not entirely indoors) must be enclosed by a perimeter fence that is of sufficient
height to keep animals and unauthorized persons out. The fence must be constructed so that it protects the animals in the
facility by restricting animals and unauthorized persons from going through it or under it and having contact with the
animals in the facility, and so that it can function as a secondary containment system for the animals in the facility. It must
be of sufficient distance (at least 3 feet) from the outside of the primary enclosure to prevent physical contact between
animals inside the enclosure and animals or persons outside the perimeter fence.

The facility failed to attain an adequate number of employees to feed and clean enclosures for 132 regulated animals.
One of the two employees present, had to delay the feeding of multiple animals to escort the APHIS inspector around the
facility for the inspection. The non-compliances identified during this inspection, as well as those identified in previous
inspection reports, are consistent with inadequate staffing levels. Without a sufficient number of adequately trained
employees, the facility cannot provide the husbandry practices necessary to maintain the animals in a manner that
ensures their health and welfare. A sufficient number of adequately trained employees shall be utilized to maintain the
professionally acceptable level of husbandry practices set forth in this subpart. Such practices shall be under a supervisor
who has a background in animal care.

The container holding water for bathing has sharp, jagged edges in two Palm cockatoo enclosures.
Birds explore and eat with their beaks, so a jagged plastic object can easily cut their beak, tongue, or mouth. Stepping on
or perching near broken edges can also injure their sensitive feet or claws, and even small cuts can lead to infection or
lameness.
The surfaces of housing facilities must be constructed in a manner and made of materials that allow them to be readily
cleaned and/or sanitized or removed and replaced when worn or soiled. Interior surfaces and surfaces that come in
contact with birds must be free of jagged edges or sharp points that could injure the birds. To be corrected this day, July
7, 2026, forward.

The facility failed to maintain the primary enclosure of four pigeons in good repair. A separate enclosure within the primary
enclosure of 4 pigeons has wire pushed out at the bottom exposing sharp, jagged points.
The birds risk injury when they crawl beneath this wire to reach the inner enclosure. Not only could it trap them in an area
with no access to water, but its sharp, jagged points can easily wound them, turning simple exploration into a harmful
situation.
Primary enclosures must be designed and constructed of suitable materials so that they are structurally sound. The
primary enclosures must be kept in good repair. Primary enclosures must be constructed and maintained so that they
have no sharp points or edges that could injure the birds. To be corrected this day, July 7, 2026, forward.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility failed to prevent the accumulation of excreta in the primary enclosures housing chickens. In the south chicken
coop, there is buildup of excreta on the walls and wooden boards constructing the walls.
Failure to clean accumulations of waste materials can increase disease hazards, attract insects, pests, and be a source of
odors.
Excreta and food waste must be removed from primary enclosures and from under and around primary enclosures as
often as necessary to prevent excessive accumulation of feces and food waste, to prevent soiling of the birds contained in
the primary enclosures, and to reduce disease hazards, insects, pests, and odors. When steam or water is used to clean
primary enclosures, measures must be taken to protect birds from being harmed, wetted involuntarily, or distressed in the
process. Standing water, except for such water in pools or other aquatic areas (e.g., ponds, waterfalls, fountains, and
other water features), must be removed from the primary enclosure. To be corrected by July 14, 2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility does not maintain an effective pest control program. Ants were observed in the food receptacles of a Rainbow
lorikeet and Umbrella cockatoo.
Keeping insects out of birds’ food dishes is important because they can contaminate the food, make it unsafe or
unappealing, and in some cases bite or sting birds, causing stress or injury. They can also introduce bacteria or mold that
increases the risk of illness. If insects overrun a dish, a bird may stop eating, which can lead to dehydration or
malnutrition, and ongoing infestations can create chronic stress that weakens a bird’s immune system and overall well
being.
A safe and effective program for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests must be
established and maintained so as to promote the health and well-being of the birds and reduce contamination by pests in
animal areas. Insecticides, chemical agents, or other pest control products that may be harmful to the birds must not be
applied to primary enclosures and other bird contact surfaces unless the application is consistent with manufacturer
recommendations or otherwise approved for use and does not harm birds. To be corrected by July 14, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with a facility representative.
